content: Microsoft Windows refers to a series of software operating systems developed by Microsoft. The first version of Windows was introduced in November 1985 as an extension to MS-DOS, designed to address the increasing demand for graphical user interfaces (GUIs). Over time, Microsoft Windows became the dominant operating system in the global personal computer market, surpassing Apple's Mac OS, which had been released earlier. By 2004, Windows held approximately 90% of the client operating system market, as stated by IDC Vice President Avneesh Saxena during the IDC Directions conference. At that time, the latest client version of Windows was Windows Vista, while the server version was Windows Server 2003. The successor to Windows Server 2003, known as Windows Server 2008, was undergoing beta testing. The term Windows encompasses various generations of Microsoft operating systems, which can be categorized as follows: 16-bit Operating Environments Early versions of Windows were often perceived as graphical user interfaces running on top of MS-DOS, relying on it for file system services. However, even the earliest 16-bit Windows versions incorporated many typical operating system functions, such as their own executable file format and device drivers for timers, graphics, printers, mice, keyboards, and sound. Unlike MS-DOS, Windows allowed users to run multiple graphical applications simultaneously through cooperative multitasking. Additionally, Windows implemented a segment-based virtual memory system, enabling it to run applications larger than the available physical memory by swapping code segments and resources in and out of memory as needed. Hybrid 16/32-bit Operating Environments Windows/386 introduced a 32-bit protected mode kernel and a virtual machine monitor, creating virtual 8086 environments for multitasking MS-DOS applications. This allowed preemptive multitasking of multiple MS-DOS environments, although graphical applications required full-screen mode. Windows applications continued to use cooperative multitasking within a single real-mode environment. Later versions, such as Windows 3.1, improved performance and memory management by introducing virtual memory and loadable virtual device drivers (VxDs), enabling better multitasking and access to extended memory. 32-bit Operating Systems The 32-bit Windows family was designed for greater reliability and business use, free from MS-DOS dependencies. Windows NT was the first in this line, introducing a new kernel and supporting multiple hardware platforms. Microsoft later aimed to unify its consumer and business operating systems, leading to the development of Windows XP, which combined the stability of the NT kernel with the user-friendly interface of Windows 95. Windows XP was released in both Home and Professional editions, with the latter offering enhanced security and networking features. 64-bit Operating Systems Windows NT initially supported 64-bit processors like DEC Alpha and MIPS R4000, although it treated them as 32-bit processors. With the advent of Intel's Itanium architecture (IA-64), Microsoft released 64-bit versions of Windows 2000, Windows XP, and Windows Server 2003. Later, support shifted to AMD64/Intel64 (x64) architectures, with the release of Windows XP Professional x64 Edition and x64 versions of Windows Server 2003. Windows Vista marked the first simultaneous release of 32-bit and x64 editions for end-users, although it did not support the Itanium architecture. History Microsoft pursued two parallel paths in operating system development: one for home users and another for professional IT users. Home versions typically emphasized multimedia support, while professional versions prioritized networking and security. Early versions of Windows, such as Windows 1.0 (1985) and Windows 2.0 (1987), extended MS-DOS functionality but lacked widespread popularity. Windows 3.0 (1990) achieved commercial success, selling 2 million copies within six months, thanks to improvements in the user interface and multitasking. Windows 95 (1995) introduced significant changes, including preemptive multitasking and a redesigned user interface. It was followed by Windows 98, which faced criticism for performance issues but improved with the release of Windows 98 Second Edition. Windows Me (2000) introduced features like System Restore but was criticized for stability issues. Windows XP (2001) combined the NT kernel's stability with the usability of Windows 95, receiving widespread acclaim. It was available in Home and Professional editions, with the latter offering advanced features. Windows Server 2003 (2003) replaced the Windows 2000 server line, focusing on security enhancements. Windows Vista (2007) introduced a redesigned interface and significant technical changes, emphasizing security. It was available in multiple editions but faced criticism for various issues. Emulation Software Several emulation tools allow users to run Windows applications without using Microsoft Windows itself. These include: Wine: An open-source implementation of the Windows API, enabling most Windows applications to run on x86-based platforms, including Linux. Wine is not an emulator but simulates the Windows environment using Windows-style APIs. CrossOver: A commercial version of Wine with licensed fonts, focusing on officially supported applications. Cedega: A proprietary fork of Wine designed for running Windows games on Linux. ReactOS: An open-source operating system aiming to run Windows software, currently in early development stages. Darwine: A project to port Wine and related tools to macOS, enabling compatibility with Windows applications. Windows Lifecycle Policy Microsoft has discontinued updates and support for many older Windows versions, including all Windows 9x versions and earlier Windows NT versions. Windows 2000 remains in extended support until July 13, 2010. Windows XP versions prior to Service Pack 2 are no longer supported, and support for Windows XP 64-bit Edition ended with the release of Windows XP Professional x64 Edition. However, users of unsupported versions can still download updates from the Windows Update catalog.
